question: Why is DMart's EBITDA margin higher than Big Bazaar's despite having a LOWER gross margin?
before: DMart owns ~90% of stores (vs Big Bazaar's leased model) avoiding escalating rents, and has ~14x inventory turnover (vs 6-8x) reducing working capital. Lower gross margin is by design — lowest prices drive footfall and volume. Tax rates don't affect EBITDA (pre-tax).
after:
Concept: EBITDA margin = EBITDA / Revenue. A lower gross margin can still yield higher EBITDA margin if operating expense leverage (from asset ownership, turnover efficiency, and scale) more than compensates. This tests understanding that margin expansion happens at the operating level, not the product level.

Why this is correct: DMart's owned-store model eliminates variable rent escalation, creating a fixed-cost advantage. Its 14x annual inventory turnover versus Big Bazaar's 6–8x means DMart converts inventory to cash much faster, reducing working capital drag and supporting higher operating leverage. These structural efficiencies allow DMart to accept lower gross margins (via everyday low prices) while still delivering superior EBITDA margins through superior cost control and asset velocity.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Tax rates do not affect EBITDA. EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, and depreciation/amortization — it is a pre-tax metric. Tax rate differences would affect net income, not EBITDA margin.

C) Charging higher prices in premium locations would raise gross margin, not lower it. The question explicitly states DMart has a lower gross margin, which is inconsistent with this option.

D) Big Bazaar's higher advertising spend is a consequence of its operational model, not the root cause of DMart's superior EBITDA margin. Advertising is captured in OpEx; the real driver is asset ownership and turnover efficiency.

Intuition: In modern retail, owning real estate and turning inventory rapidly creates structural cost advantages that dwarf product-level margin. A 1400 bps gross-margin disadvantage can be more than offset by 30–40% better asset turns and fixed-rent avoidance, producing a 300–500 bps EBITDA margin advantage. This is why DMart's low-cost, high-velocity model has proven superior to Big Bazaar's mall-based, leased-store strategy.
